Headwear: Bear/deer-hide cap: hemispherical, stitched panels, chin strap (Otzi pattern). Brown fur. TC hide band around the brow. 6-8 sided dome - no horns, no animal skulls.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Bare torso, weathered. TC hide loincloth of stitched sheepskin strips, belted. Calfskin belt ~5cm wide with a small tool pouch. Hide foot-wraps or bare feet. Read as tailored and repaired, not a single draped pelt.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: BIG stone-headed war club - polished ovoid or cushion-shaped greenstone head (fist-to-melon size, pierced straight through), wood haft ~90cm protruding both ends. Scale the head 3x the current stick tip so it reads at zoom. Flint knife at belt. No shield.
Historical Description: Neolithic / Chalcolithic Europe, c. 3300 BC. The best-evidenced Stone Age outfit anywhere is Otzi the Iceman: bearskin cap with chin strap, a goat-and-sheep-hide coat sewn from alternating dark and light strips (a natural stripe pattern), separate goatskin leggings lashed to a belt, sheepskin loincloth, and deerskin shoes on a woven bark net stuffed with grass. Five animal species, tailored, and visibly mended - the ragged-single-pelt caveman look is a myth. Perforated stone maceheads (~70mm, often chosen for striking green stone) were hafted on wood; archaeologically they read as elite status weapons rather than common issue, which suits an oversized hero club.

Headwear: Boar's-tusk helmet: tall conical / beehive cap, 3-5 dense rows of ivory-cream tusk plates with adjacent rows curving opposite ways, hinged cheek pieces, leather neck flap. Reads as a ribbed pale cone. TC on the leather chin and brow band and the cheek-piece edging.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Dendra panoply: rigid tubular bronze capsule from neck to thigh, deep bronze collar, boxy flaring stacked shoulder guards, 3 pairs of curved bronze thigh bands. Brown-gold beaten bronze - NOT yellow-gold, NOT green patina. TC wool tunic showing at the neck and below the thigh bands. Open bronze greaves; sandals or bare feet.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Bronze short sword, Naue II type: 55-65cm, straight blade tapering to a point, flanged hilt flowing straight into the blade with NO crossguard, half-moon pommel, 3-9 visible rivets. NO SHIELD - the panoply is the protection. Bronze dagger at the hip.
Historical Description: Mycenaean Greece, c. 1450-1400 BC. The Dendra panoply is roughly 15-18 hammered bronze plates thonged to a leather backing - an articulated barrel, not a fitted muscle cuirass (that is 500 years later). A 2024 study put Greek marines through 11 hours of Iliad-derived combat in a replica and confirmed it was fully combat-viable on foot, ending the old parade-armor-only theory. Boar's-tusk helmets needed the tusks of 40-50 boars, so they are inherently elite gear. Naue II swords arrived from Italy and Central Europe in the 13th c. BC and were the first Aegean blades good at both cut and thrust.

Headwear: Negau helmet: one-piece bronze dome with a raised front-to-back medial ridge (keel) and a flat, right-angle brim all the way round. Open face, no cheek pieces. Reads as a ridged bowl with a hard horizontal brim line. TC cord or pennant tied at the ridge.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Assyrian-pattern lamellar/scale corslet over a knee-length tunic: small squared-top iron plates in dense horizontal courses, torso only, arms and legs free. Cool grey iron with red-brown rust in the recesses - iron rusts brown, never green, and that is the big color separation from the Bronze Age tier. TC tunic body plus TC waist sash. Tall laced leather boots.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Longer, broader iron sword - Hallstatt C / early La Tene type, 70-85cm, straight double-edged blade visibly wider AND longer than the bronze short sword, organic wood or horn grip, iron scabbard on a hip strap. Small round Italic parma shield ~50-60cm: wood and leather, central iron boss, TC face with a simple boss-centered device.
Historical Description: A deliberate cross-culture pairing, but both halves are genuinely Iron Age. The Negau helmet is Etruscan-made, c. 450-350 BC, known from a 26-helmet hoard at Zenjak, Slovenia - a ridged dome with a flat brim, distinct from the earlier crested Villanovan type and the later knobbed Montefortino. Lamellar and scale armor of small squared plates is Neo-Assyrian, 9th-7th c. BC, using a triple-overlap system with a raised ridge on each plate to deflect. Long iron slashing swords are Hallstatt C (800-650 BC) and La Tene (450-50 BC), 60-90cm. One correction: the big oval or hexagonal shield is the Celtic form - small round shields are the Italic tradition, which is the one that belongs with a Negau helm.

Headwear: Imperial Gallic helmet: embossed eyebrow motifs on the brow, wide flared neck guard, large hinged cheek pieces, slide-on crest holder. Polished steel with brass trim and brass boss rosettes. TC crest and TC band on the brass-edged brow.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Lorica segmentata: horizontal girdle plate bands wrapping the torso, layered shoulder guards, brass buckles, lobate hinges and tie-hooks catching warm yellow highlights against bright grey-silver steel. Deliberately brighter and more polished than the Iron Age tier - the brass fittings give you the gold-trim read at zoom while staying accurate. TC tunic showing at sleeve and hem, TC focale scarf knotted at the throat. Studded leather cingulum apron hanging from the belt. Hobnailed caligae - open lattice strap boots, NOT closed shoes.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Curved rectangular scutum ~107cm tall (much larger than the Broad Swordsman's round shield): 3-ply laminated wood, canvas and calfskin cover, bronze-bound edge, big central metal boss. TC face with the Jupiter thunderbolt-and-wing blazon (the most common real one). Pompeii-type gladius: 45-50cm, parallel edges with no waist, short triangular tip - shorter than the broad sword but far cleaner and more sharply edged. Pugio dagger on the opposite hip. Optional pilum for idle poses.
Historical Description: Roman Imperial legionary, 1st-2nd c. AD. Worth knowing: lorica segmentata was probably NOT the everyday standard - mail (lorica hamata) was likely more common at all times, and segmentata may have been reserved for set-piece battles and parades. It is still the right pick here because it is the most instantly readable Roman silhouette ever made. The fittings were brass, not gold; brass gets you the warm trim you wanted without breaking accuracy. The Imperial Gallic helmet is the one with embossed eyebrows (Celtic-made, late 1st c. BC to early 2nd c. AD); the Imperial Italic is the plainer, cruder cousin. The scutum shrank from a Republican oval of ~130cm to this ~107cm curved rectangle.

Headwear: Great helm: flat-topped barrel or tapered sugarloaf, completely featureless except one horizontal vision slit and a cross of breath holes on the right side. Matte dull steel - no chrome. Worn over a mail coif and padded arming cap, so the neck reads thick. TC crest/torse at the crown and a TC painted band. The faceless blank is the strongest head silhouette in the game.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Knee-length mail hauberk with riding slits over a quilted gambeson (gambeson collar and cuffs visible at throat and wrist). Mail = flat desaturated matte grey reading as heavy dense fabric - do NOT use a specular or chrome shader. Over it, a white sleeveless surcoat to mid-calf with a bold red cross pattee, belted. TC as a broad band or quartering on the surcoat so team still reads against the white. Mail chausses on the legs, leather boots, prick spurs.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Two-handed greatsword: 1.4m+, long unsharpened ricasso for half-swording, parierhaken (hooked lugs) above the ricasso, straight quillons, pear or wheel pommel. NO SHIELD - both hands on the sword. Sheathed longsword or rondel dagger at the belt for silhouette variety.
Historical Description: This unit deliberately mixes two eras and it is worth knowing exactly where. Mail hauberk + great helm + cross surcoat is the 13th-century crusading knight (great helm c. 1210-1340; the Templar white mantle with a red cross pattee was granted in 1147). The two-handed greatsword is 16th-century - the Zweihander carried by Landsknecht Doppelsoldner, the double-pay men who walked the front of a pike block hacking down enemy pike shafts. That is roughly a 250-year gap. It looks great and it is your call; just do not let it set the era for anything else. One correction worth taking regardless: European mail was riveted, and reads as matte dull grey dense weave rather than shiny chrome - that single material choice sells medieval harder than any prop.

Headwear: Tricorne: three-sided cocked brim, black felt, edged in gold lace, TC cockade or ribbon rosette at the left cock, small white feather trim. Crisp and upright - keep it sharper than the Skirmisher's cut-down hat.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Soubreveste (cassock/tabard) worn open-sleeved over a civilian doublet: TC field carrying a large white-silver cross down front, back and both sleeves, with GOLD FLEUR-DE-LIS at each of the four arm-ends and a red flame burst at the center. Gold braid edging, red lining flashing at the openings. Knee breeches, white stockings, buckled shoes or tall leather cavalier boots. Wide leather baldric across the chest. Keep the cross white so the shape reads - TC lives in the cassock field.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Flintlock musket (Charleville pattern): walnut stock, three barrel bands, socket bayonet at the belt. Rapier on the baldric. Powder flask and cartridge box on a crossbelt. No shield. Upright drill stance.
Historical Description: Musketeers of the Guard, France, founded 1622, disbanded 1776. Two corrections to the usual picture. First, the Grey and Black musketeer companies were named for the color of their matched horses, not their uniforms - the cassock was blue. Second, the tricorne is late: the 1620s-50s D'Artagnan era wore a wide-brimmed plumed cavalier hat, and the tricorne only becomes standard from the 1660s-90s, which is exactly right for an Enlightenment slot. The cross design is authentic as described: white-silver cross, gold fleur-de-lis at the four arm-ends, red flame at the center - swapping the field for team color keeps the whole shape intact.

Headwear: Flat-topped hide skullcap, no chin strap, TC hide brow band. Keep the head shape distinct from Club Man's dome so the two Stone Age melee units separate at zoom.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Bare torso; TC hide loincloth; a single hide shoulder strap crossing the chest as a visual separator from Club Man; grass and bark foot wraps.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Long fire-hardened wooden spear, 1.9-2.5m, thickest through the forward third like a javelin, tip charred dark brown-black. Alternative: a bound flint point lashed into a split shaft with sinew and birch-tar. NO metal anywhere on this unit. Spare javelin slung on the back. No shield.
Historical Description: Paleolithic / Neolithic. The Schoningen spears from Germany are the benchmark: 1.84-2.53m of spruce, 29-47mm thick, weighted forward like a modern javelin, and thrown effectively to 15-20m in experimental tests - these were throwing weapons, not just thrusting poles. Points were fire-hardened wood; flint, bone or antler heads were lashed into a split shaft with sinew and birch-tar pitch. Flint is grey, black, honey-brown or translucent, not uniformly black - worth a small palette variation across the unit.

Headwear: Boar's-tusk helmet as the Short Swordsman, but with a plain leather neck flap and NO cheek pieces so the two Bronze Age units read apart at zoom. TC chin and brow band.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Lighter Dendra-family panoply: bronze collar and tubular torso capsule, single-piece shoulder guards (simpler than the swordsman's stacked boxy ones), 2 pairs of thigh bands. Brown-gold bronze. TC tunic at neck and hem. Open bronze greaves.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Bronze thrusting spear 2.4-3m - clearly longer than the Stone Age spear. Small socketed leaf/lozenge bronze head (keep it modest, do NOT inflate it) PLUS a bronze sauroter butt-spike at the rear, so metal glints at BOTH ends of the shaft. That two-ended metal read is the period-correct silhouette. Ash shaft ~5cm. Bronze dagger at the hip. No shield.
Historical Description: Mycenaean Greece and the Late Bronze Age Near East, c. 1700-1200 BC. The spear, not the sword, was the primary Bronze Age weapon: bronze is soft, and the long thin Type A rapiers snapped at the hilt often enough that the archaeological record is full of repairs. So a spear-first unit is arguably more accurate than the sword line. Spearheads were socketed and small relative to the shaft. The sauroter (butt-spike) counterweighted the head, let the spear be planted upright in the ground, and served as a backup point if the head sheared off.

Headwear: Negau helmet matching the Broad Swordsman, with a short TC horsehair tuft seated in the medial ridge to separate the anti-cavalry line from the melee line.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Assyrian-pattern iron scale corslet over a knee-length TC tunic with a fringed hem, wide TC waist sash, tall laced leather boots. Cool grey iron with brown rust in the recesses.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Iron-headed spear ~2.5m: longer and narrower head than the bronze version, grey steel, dark iron butt-cap. Small round Italic parma shield with a TC face and iron boss - the Bronze Age tier has no shield, so the shield IS the visible upgrade. Iron dagger at the hip.
Historical Description: Same Iron Age cross-culture pairing as the Broad Swordsman, which keeps the whole age visually coherent. The real Iron Age advantage was economic rather than mechanical: iron ore is common in places where tin (needed to make bronze) is rare and had to be traded across continents, so iron let states arm far more men rather than making each individual spear dramatically better. Visually, the whole age should swing from the Bronze Age's warm brown-gold to a cool grey-steel palette with red-brown rust in the recesses. That palette swap is the clearest you-have-advanced-an-age signal available to you, and it costs nothing in polygons.

Headwear: Corinthian helmet: a single hammered piece of bronze covering the entire head and face, with only eye slits and a narrow nose bar. Tall horsehair crest in a crest box, either fore-aft or transverse. Brown-gold bronze kept deliberately bright. TC dyed horsehair crest plus a TC band at the rim. The full-face blank is enormously readable at low poly - lean on it hard.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Bronze bell cuirass - flaring outward at the waist into a bell skirt, with stylized abstract musculature. It is the bolder low-poly shape than a muscle cuirass and is period-correct for the Archaic through early 5th c. BC. (Alternative: linen linothorax with pteruges skirt strips.) Brown-gold bronze. TC exomis tunic beneath, showing at the shoulder and as a short skirt below the cuirass. Bronze greaves sprung onto the calves - no straps needed. Sandals or bare feet.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Aspis / hoplon: deeply DISHED round shield, over 90cm across, bowl-profiled wood core with a bronze rim. Gripped by a forearm band (porpax) at the center plus a cord (antilabe) at the rim - not a fist grip. TC face with one big bold blazon: gorgon head, lion, or a simple geometric device. Doru spear 2-2.4m: ash shaft, leaf-shaped iron head, bronze sauroter. Xiphos short sword (45-60cm leaf blade) or forward-curving kopis on a baldric under the left arm.
Historical Description: Greek hoplite, c. 700-350 BC. The aspis is the defining object: over 90cm across, about 7kg, deeply bowl-shaped, and gripped by an armband at the center rather than a fist grip at the rim - which is precisely what lets it rest on the shoulder and overlap the man to the left in a phalanx. Two myths to avoid: the Spartan lambda was not used before the late 5th c. BC and most city-states had no standard blazon at all, so individual devices or plain faces are more accurate; and the Corinthian helmet probably did not originate in Corinth - it dominates Corinthian pottery because Corinth dominated pottery. Greaves were sprung to the calf and needed no straps until the 4th c. BC.

Headwear: Morion: rounded skull rising to a point at BOTH front and back, tall fore-aft comb, narrow brim turned up into a peak at each end. Bright steel. TC plume socket at the side plus a TC band. Note: a morion is always OPEN-FACED. If you want a closed face on this unit, what you actually need is a burgonet with a falling buffe.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Steel cuirass (breast and backplate) over a heavy padded gambeson whose sleeves and skirt show below. Tassets - overlapping plate thigh flaps - hanging from the fauld on sliding rivets. Bright polished steel over a TC gambeson, plus a TC sash at the waist or over one shoulder. High leather boots to the knee.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Long spear / pike 4.5-5.5m: plain ash shaft, small steel head, brass langets running down the shaft below the head, and a TC-and-gold tassel where head meets shaft. The tassel and langets give you the fancy read without inventing a fantasy spearhead - keep the head itself small and functional. Sword at the hip.
Historical Description: This is really a 16th-17th c. tercio and Landsknecht pikeman rather than a strictly medieval one, which is the right call for silhouette - a true medieval spearman is far plainer. Helmet distinctions worth having precisely: a MORION has the tall comb with the brim peaked up front and back; a CABASSET is a smooth pear-shaped skull with a small stalk at the apex and a flat narrow brim, no comb; a BURGONET has a peak over the brow, a comb, and hinged cheek pieces. Only the burgonet can be closed-faced. Pikes ran 5-7m at their peak and shortened to 4.3-4.9m by the early 18th c. Front-rank pikemen wore this cuirass-and-tasset harness while rear ranks went much lighter.

Headwear: Burgonet with a falling buffe: comb over the crown, peak over the brow, hinged cheek pieces, and a face plate closing the front. This is the historically real way to get the closed-face look you described - a morion cannot close. Blackened steel with heavy gold-etched bands. TC plume at the comb, TC cheek-piece lining.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Brigandine: small steel plates riveted INSIDE a fabric shell, so the outside shows a dense grid of gilt rivet heads over rich cloth. TC velvet or heavy wool shell, gold rivets in tight rows, gold lace edging. Steel pauldrons with gold etching at the shoulders. Slashed-and-puffed doublet sleeves in TC and gold beneath. Knee breeches, stockings, buckled shoes.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Halberd 2.0-2.5m: broad axe blade one side, straight thrusting spike continuing the shaft line at the top, rear fluke/beak opposite the blade for hooking riders down. Blued steel head with gold etching, brass langets, TC-and-gold tassel at the head. Sword at the hip. No shield.
Historical Description: Brigandine construction IS the visual: 15th-16th c. armor of small oblong steel plates riveted to the inside of a cloth or leather garment, so what shows outside is a pattern of rivet studs - 15th c. examples group rivets in threes, 16th c. examples run them in dense rows, and gilt embossed rivets over velvet were genuinely used for status. Halberd anatomy is fixed by the 15th c.: axe blade, top spike, rear fluke. Two myths to skip: the Vatican Swiss Guard's famous striped uniform was designed in 1914 by Commandant Jules Repond, not in the 16th century and certainly not by Michelangelo. And, again, a morion is open-faced by definition - the burgonet-with-buffe above gets you what you actually wanted.

Headwear: Plain low hide skullcap with a TC band, or bare-headed with a TC leather headband. Keep the profile low so the sling's arc owns the silhouette.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Bare torso; TC hide loincloth; a leather ammo pouch slung across the body on a strap - the pouch is the unit's read when idle. Bare feet.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Sling: TWO long braided cords, one ending in a wrist or finger retention loop and the other in a release tab, meeting at a small diamond-shaped leather pouch. It must NOT be a Y-frame slingshot - that is a 19th-century AD invention and the single most common mistake in this weapon. Cords wrap around the wrist when idle. Ammo: rounded river stones 50-200g in the belt pouch. Flint knife. No shield.
Historical Description: Sling-stones appear in the Near East by the 6th millennium BC; the oldest surviving slings are Egyptian plaited flax and bast fiber, c. 2000-1800 BC. Cords were braided rather than twisted, because braid does not stretch and untwist - that is what makes the weapon accurate. River stones were the default ammunition; cast lead bullets (glandes), sometimes inscribed with curses or unit marks, are a later Greek and Roman refinement. Trained slingers, the Balearic mercenaries above all, were serious battlefield specialists with lethal range, not shepherds with a toy.

Headwear: Leather cap: close-fitting, low, stitched panels, short neck flap, TC band around the brow. Black tight-curled hair beneath, with a white cloth headband over the cap as an accent.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Bare torso; wrapped linen kilt over a woven belt - natural cream linen with a TC geometric-patterned center flap and hem band, so the flap is where team color lives. Animal-skin and woven-wool mantle over one shoulder for texture. Small leather bracer tied to the left forearm. Metal armbands and a bead collar. Barefoot.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Self bow 1-1.5m: plain wood, double-curved decurved tips. Tapered leather quiver tube with a cap, slung on the back, fletching showing. Bundle of spare arrows held in the off hand for the idle pose. Bronze dagger. No shield.
Historical Description: Egyptian and Nubian archery, New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC - Nubia was literally called Ta-Seti, Land of the Bow. The best surviving visual reference is the 11th Dynasty model army of 40 Nubian archers from the tomb of Mesehti at Asyut (Cairo, JE 30969): red kilts with green geometric patterning and a decorated center flap, black curly wigs, white headbands, anklets and necklaces, all barefoot, each holding a bow in one hand and a bundle of arrows in the other. Small leather wrist bracers have been found still tied to soldiers' arms in mass graves at Deir el-Bahri. The simple self bow was the regular infantry weapon; the composite bow was elite and chariot gear, which is why it belongs to the next tier up.

Headwear: Tall pointed bronze conical helmet: smooth cone, short neck flap, TC-dyed plume at the tip and a TC band at the rim. This hard pointed cone is the Assyrian signature and separates the tier from the Bronze Age leather cap instantly.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Knee-length TC tunic with a heavy fringed hem and a wide TC waist sash. Iron scale corslet over chest and back ONLY - limbs completely free. Tall laced leather boots to mid-calf. Cool grey iron scale under a brown-gold bronze helmet gives you two distinct metals on one unit, which is a cheap way to make the tier look richer.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Angular composite bow: the limbs meet in a shallow V with reflexed tips that stay curved even at full draw - distinct from a smooth C-curve recurve, and a strong period marker. Quiver on the back with fletching showing, second bow case at the hip. Iron dagger. No shield - though the historical version pairs the archer with a shield-bearer holding a full-height standing pavise, which is a great option if you ever want a paired unit.
Historical Description: Neo-Assyrian archer, 9th-7th c. BC - the most-depicted archer of the ancient world, from the Nimrud and Nineveh palace reliefs. Those reliefs consistently show archers working in two-man teams, with a second soldier holding a tall standing shield for cover while the archer draws. The Assyrian bow descends from the Egyptian angular bow but adds reflexed tips: shorter, more efficient and better suited to chariot and mounted use. Scale armor covered the torso only, worn over a tunic and leaving the limbs free, and the tall pointed bronze helmet is the unmistakable signature of the army.

Headwear: Pilos: brimless conical FELT cap, undyed cream or TC-dyed, soft-looking with a slight forward lean. Alternative: the Macedonian kausia, a broad flat-crowned felt hat. Keep it soft and brimless so it contrasts with the Iron Age tier's hard metal cone.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Exomis - short tunic with the RIGHT shoulder seam left unpinned to free the draw arm. This is both historically correct for light troops and a great asymmetric silhouette. TC cloth in linen or crimson wool, belted at the waist, hem at mid-thigh. Bare legs, light sandals or bare feet. No armor at all - mobility is the read.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Composite bow: wood core, horn belly, sinew back, deep recurve. Small round shield ~40-50cm SLUNG from a belt at the hip or on the back rather than carried in hand, TC face. Light axe or short xiphos as backup. Hip quiver.
Historical Description: Cretan archers, 5th c. BC onward - the most sought-after light missile troops in the ancient world, hired by Greek city-states, by Alexander, by Rome down to at least 161 AD, and by Byzantium as late as 1453. They fought largely unarmored for mobility, with a small round shield slung on a belt and a light axe for close work. The exomis is a genuine working garment: two rectangles sewn into a cylinder with the right shoulder left open so the arm can move freely. The pilos was the ordinary felt cap of travelers, workmen and sailors; note that the popular idea of a standardized Spartan pilos helmet is not well supported by evidence.

Headwear: Chaperon hood in Lincoln green with a long liripipe tail hanging down the back, worn over a small TC coif. The pointed hood plus trailing tail is a strong, instantly readable silhouette and does the Robin Hood job better than the hat does.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Green wool cotehardie to mid-thigh over a TC gambeson body, TC belt with a hanging pouch; hose in a contrasting color; ankle turnshoes. Short green cape or shoulder mantle. Put TC in the tunic field or a bold TC quartering and keep green as the accent, so the Robin Hood read survives team coloring.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Steel-prod crossbow with a foot STIRRUP at the muzzle end and a GOAT'S-FOOT LEVER hooked on the belt for spanning. Bolt quiver: a short boxy belt-mounted case of wood and hide holding a dozen 30-40cm bolts with short leather or wooden vanes - NOT a long arrow quiver on the back. Falchion or dagger at the hip. Optional: tall TC pavise shield with a central ridge, propped on its spike.
Historical Description: One honest note up front: Robin Hood was a longbowman, and the matched green hood-and-tunic uniform is a modern costume convention crystallized by 19th-century illustrators and cemented by the 1938 Errol Flynn film - the medieval ballads do not describe it, and the 18th-c. Robin Hood's Garland actually puts Robin himself in scarlet with his band in green. Lincoln green is real, though: a genuine Lincoln-made dyed wool, woad blue overdyed with weld yellow, named in print from 1510. Hoods with liripipes were universal medieval headwear across every class. The crossbow kit is fully accurate - stirrup and goat's-foot for field troops, windlass or cranequin for heavy siege bows, short belt-box quivers for bolts, and a pavise held by a partner while the shooter reloads. The Genoese crossbowmen lost at Crecy in 1346 partly because their pavises were still back in the baggage train.

Headwear: Deliberately irregular across the unit - a cut-down tricorne with a TC plume, a jockey cap, or a Scotch bonnet. Use the plumed cut-down tricorne as the hero read: brim trimmed shorter and cocked less crisply than the Musketeer's, so the two silhouettes separate at a glance.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Short green wool coat or sleeved waistcoat, double-breasted, white-metal buttons, cut short and close for movement. GREEN as the base with TC on the facings, cuffs, collar and a TC sash - the exact inverse of the Musketeer, whose whole torso is TC. Green wool leggings buttoned up the outside; moccasins or plain shoes. Blanket roll across the back.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Flintlock firelock, shorter than the Musketeer's. Tomahawk / hatchet at the belt, scalping knife, powder horn slung under the RIGHT arm, leather bullet bag buckled at the waist. No bayonet, no shield. Pose low and half-crouched against the Musketeer's upright drill stance.
Historical Description: Rogers' Rangers, French and Indian War, c. 1755-1763. Documented from deserter advertisements, standing orders and Captain Knox's journal: short green coats or sleeved waistcoats in cheap green Bath Rug cloth with green serge lining and white-metal buttons, green leggings, and - importantly - MIXED headwear, with jockey caps, cut-down hats and Scotch bonnets all recorded rather than a uniform tricorne. Kit was firelock, tomahawk, scalping knife, powder horn under the right arm and bullet bag at the waist. The crisp fringed hunting shirt everyone pictures is real but later and different: that is 1770s Revolutionary War rifleman dress from the Virginia and Pennsylvania backcountry, not Rogers' 1750s green wool. Irregularity is the accurate look here, so vary the unit rather than uniforming it.

Headwear: Simple low leather cap, close-fitting and stitched, TC band; or a folded cloth head-wrap. Nothing metal anywhere on the head.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Sleeveless leather jerkin over a short TC tunic, cut for lightness. Leather belt, bare arms, short leather boots or wrapped foot bindings. Everything trimmed close - no hanging cloth to break the silhouette. Speed should read from the outline alone.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Light wooden javelin/spear with a small bronze or fire-hardened tip. Hide water skin and small pack. No shield, no armor. HORSE: ride bareback or on a simple folded cloth pad - no saddle tree, and NO STIRRUPS (they do not exist yet). Rope halter and simple bit. Rebuild the horse mesh properly: deeper chest, defined croup, real neck crest, mane and tail as flat alpha cards or low-poly geo strips, 8-sided leg tapers.
Historical Description: Bronze Age riders existed only as individual elite messengers and scouts; organized cavalry does not appear until the Neo-Assyrian reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II, 883-859 BC, and even those men ride bareback in pairs with one holding both sets of reins. On the horse size: your instinct to enlarge it is right for gameplay, but worth doing knowingly. Real Bronze Age horses stood about 129-137cm at the withers (12.2-13.2 hands) - pony-sized - and even medieval warhorses were mostly under 147cm. Doubling that gives you a horse larger than any that has ever existed, so scale instead to roughly a modern 15-16 hand riding horse: it reads big and heroic next to the historical pony, keeps the rider in proportion, and stays defensible. Also note stirrups are a Chinese invention (c. 302 AD) that only reach Europe around the 7th-8th c. AD - nothing before the Medieval age should have them.

Headwear: Open-faced kettle hat (wide-brimmed steel war hat) or a plain conical helm over a mail coif. Open face, so it reads clearly apart from the Knight's closed visor. TC band around the brim, small TC pennon at the crown.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Mail haubergeon to mid-thigh - shorter and lighter than the Knight's hauberk - in matte grey, over a TC quilted gambeson whose sleeves and skirt show. Short TC surcoat with side slits. Mail or cloth chausses, riding boots, prick spurs. Deliberately NO plate anywhere on this unit.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Light lance with a TC pennon - the pennon is the unit's read at distance. Sword at the hip, small heater shield in TC. Alternative Turcopole variant: composite bow and hip quiver instead of the lance. HORSE: no caparison, plain leather harness, TC saddle cloth only. Lighter and leggier than the Knight's mount.
Historical Description: Hobelars and Turcopoles are the real medieval scout cavalry. Hobelars are English and Irish, first documented in 1296 and standard in English forces from about 1300; the 1335 English kit was an aketon or plates, a basinet or open palet helm, gorget and iron gauntlets, riding a small agile Irish hobby of 12-14 hands. Robert the Bruce used them for raids of 60-70 miles a day. Turcopoles served the Crusader States from 1096 to the fall of Acre in 1291: quilted gambeson rather than mail, conical helmet, lance and composite bow, on lighter local horses. Either way the read is identical - visibly lighter and leaner than a knight, no plate, no heraldic horse cloth, smaller mount.

Headwear: Crew: linen headband or a short striped cloth head covering with a TC band; bare-headed with a black wig is equally correct. Keep both crewmen's heads low-profile so the chariot itself owns the silhouette.

Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Two-horse light chariot. SIX-SPOKE wheels (four-spoke on early examples). Axle set at the EXTREME REAR of the cab - that is the distinctive Egyptian trait, it widens the stance and reads fast. D-shaped open cab of bent-wood frame with stretched WOVEN-LEATHER MESH sides and a woven leather strip floor; no seat, both crew stand. Central draft pole curving up to a yoke bar across both horses' necks. Two crossed leather quiver cases (arrows plus bow case) mounted outside the cab in TC. Crew of two: driver with reins, archer with composite bow. TC on cab panel, quiver cases and horse plumes.
Historical Description: Egyptian New Kingdom chariot, c. 1550-1070 BC, 18th-20th Dynasty - the best silhouette available for this slot. Wheels went from four spokes in the early 18th Dynasty to a standard six by Thutmose III; Tutankhamun's surviving chariots are six-spoke. The rear-set axle is the diagnostic Egyptian feature and it made a wide, stable shooting platform. The Hittite alternative carried three men (driver, shield-bearer, spearman), set the axle at the center, and was correspondingly heavier and slower - use that design if you ever want a heavy chariot variant. The cab was bent wood covered in woven leather mesh rather than solid panels, which flexed as suspension. Crew of two, both aristocrats: the kedjen drove, the menyt shot.

Headwear: Tall pointed bronze conical helmet with a short neck guard and hinged flaps. TC plume or crest at the apex, TC band at the rim.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Iron or bronze scale corslet over a knee-length TC tunic with a fringed hem; wide TC sash; tall laced leather boots. TORSO ARMOR ONLY - arms and legs bare or cloth-covered. Trim, banded and angular; nothing should hang loose.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Long thrusting spear/lance held OVERHAND (no stirrups means no couched charge), plus a composite bow and hip quiver; akinakes short sword at the belt. Optional small round shield in TC. HORSE: completely UNARMORED - this is the critical visual contrast against the Cataphract. Saddle CLOTH only, fringed and TC-patterned, with no saddle tree; bridle with decorative bronze bosses; forehead plume. No stirrups.
Historical Description: Neo-Assyrian and Median cavalry, 8th-7th c. BC. The evolution is easy to show on screen: 9th-century Assyrian riders are unarmored, bareback, and work in pairs with one man holding both sets of reins while the other shoots. By the time of Sargon II and Sennacherib, riders control their own mounts, sit on saddle cloths, and wear scale corslets like the infantry. Crucially the horse itself stays unarmored throughout - keep it that way, because that is exactly what makes the Classical-age Cataphract land as a genuine upgrade rather than a reskin. And no stirrups: they do not reach the Near East until roughly the 7th-8th c. AD, so the rider grips with the legs and the seat reads more forward and upright.

Headwear: Full face-covering helmet - a smooth metal mask with narrow eye slits and a nose ridge, often with a mail aventail to the shoulders. Blank and inhuman; that is the entire point. TC crest or small TC pennant at the crown, TC edging on the aventail.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Head-to-ankle scale armor: roughly 1,300 small overlapping scales, 1-2mm thick, laced and sewn to a leather backing, covering torso, ARMS AND LEGS - the silhouette is uniformly geometric with no exposed cloth or skin anywhere. Mail beneath at the joints. TC tabard band across the chest and a TC sash at the waist. Scale boots.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Kontos lance ~4m, gripped TWO-HANDED so there is NO SHIELD - historically correct and a strong distinctive pose. Iron point. A strap or chain runs from the horse's harness to the rider, transferring the charge's momentum into the thrust. Sword and mace at the belt. HORSE: SECTIONAL scale barding - separate armored panels for head (chamfron), neck, chest and flanks, not one continuous suit - with TC caparison edging and a TC plume on the chamfron.
Historical Description: Parthian and Sassanid cataphracts, c. 323 BC to 651 AD, adopted by the Seleucids after Alexander. A full suit ran about 1,300 scales and 40kg, wired and sewn onto a hide backing. The horse's barding is sectional - separate scale panels for head, neck, chest and flanks - which is worth modeling as distinct pieces because it reads as real armor rather than a texture. The kontos was held in both hands with no shield, and a strap linking rider to harness let the horse's mass rather than the arm deliver the blow. Rider and horse both fully scaled with a blank masked face is the most alien, least human silhouette in the ancient world, which is exactly what the age's shock unit should be.

Headwear: Bascinet with a hounskull (pig-faced pointed) visor and a mail aventail over the shoulders. The pointed snout gives a sharper, more aggressive read than the Vanguard's flat great helm, so your two medieval heavies stay distinct. Bright polished steel; TC crest and TC edging on the aventail's cloth border.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Full plate harness: cuirass, fauld and tassets, pauldrons, articulated arm and leg harness, sabatons. Bright polished steel - brighter and smoother than any earlier armor in the game. TC surcoat/jupon fitted over the breastplate, TC belt. Matte grey mail voiders showing at the armpits and groin; that contrast between matte mail and bright plate is what sells the material.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Couched lance with a vamplate hand-guard, painted in a TC-and-heraldic spiral. Arming sword and rondel dagger at the belt. Small heater shield in TC with one bold charge. HORSE: full heraldic caparison in TC covering the body to the fetlocks, steel chamfron on the head, TC plume. Biggest, heaviest mount in the game - deepest chest, thickest legs.
Historical Description: Western European knight, 15th c. for the full plate. Keep the timeline straight: mail alone through the 13th c., transitional mail-and-plate c. 1330s-1410s, and full plate harness only from about the 1420s. The hounskull-visored bascinet is the quintessential Hundred Years' War head, c. 1360-1420 (Agincourt, 1415). The heraldic caparison peaks in the 13th-14th c. and is off real battlefields by the early 15th, surviving in tournaments - so a full-plate knight in a caparison compresses eras slightly, but it is a very common and very readable compression. On the horse: the destrier was a prime charger costing seven or eight times an ordinary horse, but recent archaeology finds most medieval warhorses stood under 147cm, smaller than the popular image. Scale it up for readability, just know you are doing it.

Headwear: Tricorne with TC cockade and gold lace edging, over a queued wig. Late-period alternative: crested brass helmet with a fur turban and horsehair mane (French, 1762 onward - do not use it for anything earlier).
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Long-skirted TC uniform coat with contrasting facings on cuffs and lapels, gold buttons in pairs; TC waistcoat; buff leather breeches; HEAVY THIGH-HIGH BLACK RIDING BOOTS with spurs - the boots are the single clearest mounted-infantry tell against the Musketeer's buckled shoes. White crossbelts over the chest.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Short flintlock carbine / musketoon carried on a shoulder-belt swivel or in a saddle boot. Straight sword at the hip, pair of pistols in pommel holsters. HORSE: military saddle with pommel holsters, blanket roll or valise at the cantle, TC shabraque (saddle cloth) with gold lace edging and a corner device. NO barding - this age's cavalry is fast and unarmored.
Historical Description: Dragoons emerged in the early 17th century as mounted infantry - men who rode to the fight and dismounted to shoot - and were organized and ranked as infantry rather than cavalry. The carbine or musketoon is the defining weapon; French dragoons carried a blunderbuss called a dragon, which may be where the name comes from. Early dragoons wore a soft cloth cap, sometimes fur-fronted, specifically so a slung musket strap would clear the head; the tricorne takes over through the 18th century, and the crested brass helmet with fur turban and horsehair mane is a late arrival (French, 1762). By the later 1700s dragoons functioned as ordinary line cavalry despite the name.

Headwear: Shaved head with ONE long braided sidelock hanging over the right ear to the shoulder - the sem-priest's mark, and a genuinely distinctive head silhouette (a bald head alone reads as nothing at zoom). Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Leopard pelt draped over the LEFT shoulder, paws tied across the chest, head and tail hanging - tawny gold with black rosettes. The asymmetric drape is what gives the silhouette. Beneath it, a bleached white pleated linen kilt to mid-calf and a broad beaded collar. TC on the sash under the pelt and in the collar's bead rows. Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Was-staff, or a long ritual censer with a curling smoke wisp (the smoke doubles as your heal VFX anchor). Small libation vessel at the belt. Nothing weaponlike anywhere. Pelt plus sidelock plus staff should say holy man at any zoom level. No shield.
Historical Description: Egyptian sem-priest, attested from roughly 3000 BC through the Roman period, chosen here because the spotted pelt is the most unmistakable priest read in the ancient world. Two details worth having right: the sem-priest who performed the Opening of the Mouth ceremony is identified in the record by the sidelock of youth rather than a shaven head, while full body-shaving is a separate and well-attested general priestly purity practice (Herodotus says priests shaved every other day). Combining the two is defensible and the sidelock gives you a silhouette a bald head cannot. The main alternative is the Roman flamen, whose apex - an olive-wood spike on a wool cap, legally required to be worn in public, and disqualifying if it fell off mid-rite - is arguably an even stronger shape at small scale, though it gives up the pelt's color read.

An open turret rises ~3m above the roof with an archer inside. A ~5m ram beam HANGS ON ROPES from the roof frame and swings pendulum-style rather than being pushed rigid. The head is a metal-plated CHISEL/BLADE shape for prying mudbrick courses apart - not a blunt knob and not a ram's-head casting. TC on the roof banner, turret shield panel and hide side-curtains.
Historical Description: Neo-Assyrian siege ram, 9th-7th c. BC, from the Nimrud reliefs of Ashurnasirpal II (883-859 BC) and the Lachish reliefs of Sennacherib (the siege of 701 BC) - the earliest well-depicted siege engine anywhere in the world. Ashurnasirpal's type runs on six wheels with a raised turret for an archer giving covering fire; by Sennacherib's time they get lighter, drop to four wheels, and are deployed in multiples against one stretch of wall. The beam hung from ropes so it swung, and the head was a bladed chisel for gouging mudbrick apart rather than a blunt hammer. Wicker and hide covering, often wetted, was the standard anti-incendiary measure of the period.

Headwear: Crew: tricorne with TC cockade; gunner in a leather apron.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Crew: TC coat with contrasting facings, waistcoat, knee breeches, black campaign gaiters buttoned up the outside (white gaiters are parade dress - black hid dirt in the field).
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Gribeauval-pattern field gun. Tapered cast BRONZE barrel - warm amber-brown patinating to dark olive, NOT bright toy-gold and NOT rust-brown - with integral trunnions seated in the carriage cheeks and an elevating SCREW at the breech. Two-wheeled wooden carriage, ~146cm wheels with iron tires, long trail. Separate two-wheeled limber with an ammunition chest hooks to the trail for towing. Rammer, sponge, worm and linstock racked on the carriage; shot pyramid alongside. TC on carriage woodwork, limber chest and crew coats.
Historical Description: Gribeauval system, French royal ordinance of 3 October 1774, in service from 1776 through the Napoleonic Wars - the first artillery built to standardized calibers (4-, 8- and 12-pounder plus a 6-inch howitzer) with interchangeable parts across the whole train. Field and siege guns were high-tin bronze; iron was reserved for mortars. That material choice matters for your palette: bronze reads warm brown-gold to olive patina, while the cast-iron guns of other national systems read matte black-charcoal. Getting that tone wrong is the most common cannon error in games. Field guns used a screw for elevation with about 8 degrees of range; older siege patterns used wooden quoin wedges instead.

Headwear: Crew: Assyrian-pattern pointed bronze conical helmets with TC plumes, matching the Battering Ram so the siege tier reads as one set.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Crew: fringed knee-length TC tunics, iron scale corslets, tall laced leather boots.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Two-armed torsion stone-thrower (lithobolos / palintone). Heavy tan-brown weathered timber A-frame with TWO VERTICAL SPRING FRAMES, each holding a thick bundle of off-white twisted sinew rope - give those bundles real geometry, because the twisted rope IS the visual identity of a torsion engine. Two throwing arms swing inward to a central bowstring; long stock/slider down the middle with a winch and pawl at the rear; stone ball in the cradle. Iron fittings dark grey-black. TC on painted frame panels and a banner on the rear post.
Historical Description: Honest flag: there were no catapults of any kind in the Iron Age. The earliest mechanical artillery is the Greek gastraphetes, a belly-braced composite bow on a stock, from before about 420 BC. The oxybeles follows around 375 BC, and true torsion engines powered by twisted sinew springs arrive about 340 BC under Philip II's engineers, with the first hard evidence in an Athenian arsenal inventory of 338-326 BC. So this engine sits roughly 300 years ahead of its slot. Two clean ways to handle it: keep the torsion design and accept the anachronism, since it looks right and players will read it as generic ancient siege; or swap it for an Assyrian wheeled siege tower or a stone-lobbing crew, which is genuinely 8th-7th c. BC. Also worth knowing for later: the one-armed Roman onager everyone pictures is late, first described in 353 AD, so it is wrong for a legionary-era Roman unit too.

Headwear: Crew: chaperon hoods in TC wool; the master carpenter in a coif and flat cap.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Crew: TC wool tunics to the knee, hose, leather aprons, turnshoes. Engineers and carpenters, not soldiers.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Counterweight trebuchet. Tall stout timber A-frame in weathered grey-brown with dark iron-strapped joints. Beam up to ~15m pivoting on a high axle; the short end carries a large iron-banded timber COUNTERWEIGHT BOX, hinged so it swings, filled with stone; the long end carries a hemp rope sling with a fixed release hook. Winch, rope and pawl at the base, ladder up the frame. TC on painted frame panels, the counterweight box face and a banner at the top of the A-frame.
Historical Description: The counterweight trebuchet is genuinely medieval - first clearly described in 1187 by Mardi ibn Ali al-Tarsusi writing about Saladin's siege engines, with the exact point of invention still disputed between Byzantine, Crusader and Islamic Mediterranean engineers. European peak use is 13th-15th c.; Edward I's Warwolf at Stirling Castle in 1304 is the famous example. Do not confuse it with the earlier traction trebuchet, which is Chinese, attested by the 4th c. BC, and powered by a team hauling ropes on the short arm - visually that one has a fan of pull-ropes and a visible crew, while yours has a big hinged weight box and a winch. Gunpowder made the whole type obsolete by the 15th-16th c.

Headwear: Crew: tricorne with TC cockade, as the Cannon crew.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Crew: TC coat with contrasting facings, waistcoat, breeches, black gaiters, gunner's leather apron.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: LONG, SLENDER gun - barrel length is the entire read. 25-32 calibers long, visibly thinner and much longer than the Cannon's tapered field piece so the two never get confused in a build menu. Cast bronze in warm amber-brown with olive patina, or matte black-charcoal cast iron for the cheaper variant. Reinforcing rings and dolphin lifting handles along the barrel, trunnions at the balance point. Heavier siege carriage with larger wheels, or a low four-wheeled naval truck carriage for the emplaced look. QUOIN WEDGE under the breech rather than an elevating screw. Rammer, sponge and shot pyramid alongside. TC on carriage timbers.
Historical Description: The culverin is a Renaissance and early-modern gun, developed in the late 15th c. and in main service through the 16th-17th c. It is defined by proportion rather than caliber: a barrel 25-32 calibers long against a standard cannon's short thick tube. That geometry buys velocity, flat trajectory and range at the cost of raw wall-smashing power - which is why culverins and demi-culverins were the English long-range naval guns against the Spanish Armada in 1588, engaging out to around 2,000 yards, and why in siege work they fired roughly eight aimed rounds an hour against defenders and works rather than battering the wall itself.

Headwear: Hide skullcap, or bare head with a TC hide headband. Hair loose with a matted texture rather than styled.

Separate hide leggings tied up to the belt. TC loincloth or belt-cloth. Bark-net and hide shoes stuffed with grass.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Antler pick, flint axe, woven grass carry-basket, birch-bark container, digging stick. Work poses: knapping flint, hauling a bundle, tending a hearth, scraping a hide on a frame.
Historical Description: Otzi the Iceman (c. 3300 BC) sets the standard and it is worth using: a goat-and-sheep-hide coat sewn from alternating dark and light strips into a natural stripe, separate goatskin leggings lashed to a belt, a sheepskin loincloth, a calfskin belt with a tool pouch, and deerskin-and-bearskin shoes built on a woven linden-bark net stuffed with grass insulation. Five animal species, tailored, and visibly repaired with grass-fiber stitching. The single-draped-fur caveman look is wrong - Stone Age clothing was technical, and showing that is both more accurate and more interesting to look at.

Headwear: Bare head with short cropped dark hair, or a folded linen head-cloth with a TC band. Women: a simple linen headband.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Natural CREAM linen wrap kilt (schenti) belted at the waist - plain and short for laborers - with a TC sash or TC-patterned hem band; bare torso; barefoot. Women: ankle-length linen sheath dress on shoulder straps with a TC shawl. Keep linen off-white and undyed, not bleached bright white.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Bronze sickle, hoe, woven reed basket, shoulder yoke carrying two water jars, pottery amphora, mudbrick mould.
Historical Description: Egypt and the Aegean, c. 1550-1100 BC. The schenti kilt was worn by every social class - what changed with rank was fabric fineness, pleating and length, not the shape of the garment. So distinguish villagers from elites through cloth quality and accessories rather than a different silhouette. Linen was almost always left undyed, giving you an off-white, cream and pale-tan palette rather than bright colors. Most people went barefoot day to day, with reed or leather sandals reserved for occasions, and heads were commonly shaved for lice control with wigs kept for formal wear.

Headwear: Undyed wool cap or a simple hood; hair tied back; TC headband or cap band.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Knee-length wool tunic, undyed or madder-dyed, with a TC waist sash and a fringed hem; wool trousers or bare legs; leather belt; laced leather shoes or short boots. A CHECKED or striped wool cloak pinned at one shoulder with a bronze fibula - woven check is a real Iron Age textile signature and reads beautifully at low resolution.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Iron sickle, iron-shod spade, hand quern, wool distaff and spindle, iron axe, wicker hurdle panels.
Historical Description: Iron Age Europe and the Near East, c. 800-500 BC. The meaningful change this age is economic: iron ore is widespread in places where tin for bronze was rare and had to be traded across continents, so ordinary farmers get metal tools for the first time. A villager holding an iron sickle rather than a bronze one is a genuine historical upgrade, not just a prop swap. Woven checks and stripes in madder red, weld yellow, woad blue and undyed brown-grey are all well attested in surviving Iron Age textiles, so the civilian palette can get noticeably more colorful this age even as the military palette goes cold grey.

Headwear: Conical brimless felt pilos cap in undyed cream, or a broad straw sun hat for field workers. TC band.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Exomis - short tunic with the right shoulder unpinned, freeing the working arm and giving a strong asymmetric silhouette - in natural linen or TC wool, belted at the waist, hem at mid-thigh. Bare legs, leather sandals or bare feet. Short cloak on some variants.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Iron sickle and pruning hook, mattock, amphora, wicker basket, handcart, mason's mallet and chisel, surveying groma for the builder variant.
Historical Description: Greek and Roman working dress, c. 500 BC-300 AD. The exomis is specifically the garment of laborers and light infantry: two rectangles sewn into a cylinder with the right shoulder seam left open or pinned so the working arm is free - which is why the same cut shows up on your Composite Archer. The pilos was the ordinary brimless felt cap of travelers, workmen and sailors. Roman farm work centered on the villa rustica, an estate deliberately split between the owner's residence and the working half of barns, presses, stables and quarters.

Headwear: Chaperon hood with a short liripipe, or a coif tied under the chin; straw hat for harvest workers. TC on the hood. Women: linen wimple or veil.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: Wool cotehardie/tunic to the knee over a linen shirt, TC field, leather belt with a hanging pouch; wool hose; ankle-length turnshoes. Apron on craft variants. Women: long wool kirtle, TC apron. Visible patching and mending is accurate and adds character at no polygon cost.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Scythe, flail, wooden bucket yoke, axe and adze, carpenter's saw, handcart, sack of grain, shepherd's crook.
Historical Description: Western Europe, c. 1100-1450. Peasant dress is genuinely simple - a belted wool tunic over a linen shirt, hose, and turnshoes, made sole-inward and then turned right side out - and the hood with a liripipe tail was universal headwear across every class. Cloth was a household's largest expense after food, so garments were patched, re-dyed and handed down for years; visible mending is historically correct rather than a shortcut. These are the villagers who belong beside the tithe barn and the timber-framed jettied house.

Headwear: Round-crowned felt hat with a modest brim, or a knitted wool cap; women in a linen mob cap. TC hat band.
Body Garment / Leg / Footwear: TC wool waistcoat over a linen shirt with sleeves rolled; knee breeches, wool stockings, buckled leather shoes; canvas or leather work apron. Women: linen shift, TC petticoat and bodice, apron, neckerchief.
Signature Props (Items, Weapons, Shields: Iron-shod spade, scythe, flail, wooden wheelbarrow, hand-cranked winnowing fan, cooper's tools and barrel, sack truck, seed drill for the farm variant.
Historical Description: Britain and colonial America, 17th-18th c., during the agricultural revolution. This is the age when farm work begins to mechanize: Andrew Meikle's threshing machine of 1786 and the enclosure-driven model farms with purpose-built cattle byres and field barns change the whole working landscape. The threshing barn is the signature structure - a large aisled barn with opposing wagon doors deliberately aligned to the prevailing wind, so the draft blowing through the open doorway winnows chaff from grain on the threshing floor. Working dress is waistcoat, shirt, breeches and stockings, with a canvas or leather apron varying by trade.
